title: 1 Chronicles 12:1–15
context: The Chronicler now goes back in time to the men who joined David before he became king. While he was at Ziklag as a fugitive from Saul, ambidextrous archers and slingers from Benjamin, Saul’s own tribe, came to him. Gadite warriors crossed the flooded Jordan in the first month to join him at the stronghold in the wilderness, described as having faces like lions and being swift as gazelles. The lists show support for David gathering from many tribes, including Saul’s relatives, long before all Israel made him king.

verses.text: Now these are those who came to David to Ziklag while he was a fugitive from Saul the son of Kish. They were among the mighty men, his helpers in war.
verses.arminianNotes: These men came to David at Ziklag while he was a fugitive from Saul. Arminian readers note that they chose to join David during his hardest years, before there was any guarantee of success.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God gathering support for David in advance of his kingship. Shared ground: Ziklag was given to David by Achish of Gath (1 Samuel 27:6), and its exact site is debated; both traditions read the verse as honoring early loyalty.

verses.text: They were armed with bows, and could use both the right hand and the left in slinging stones and in shooting arrows from the bow. They were of Saul’s relatives of the tribe of Benjamin.
verses.arminianNotes: The men are ambidextrous archers and slingers from Benjamin, Saul’s own relatives. Arminian readers note the significance of Saul’s kin choosing David, a choice that may have cost them standing with their tribe.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God turning hearts even within Saul’s family toward David. Both traditions note the skill described, recalling the left-handed Benjamites of Judges 20:16, and read the verse as showing growing support.

verses.text: The chief was Ahiezer, then Joash, the sons of Shemaah the Gibeathite; Jeziel and Pelet, the sons of Azmaveth; Beracah; Jehu the Anathothite;
verses.arminianNotes: The chief is Ahiezer, then Joash, sons of Shemaah the Gibeathite, and others including Jehu the Anathothite. Arminian readers note that the Chronicler names the leaders individually, honoring each one.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the names a record of those God raised up to stand with David. Shared ground: the Gibeathite is likely from Gibeah, Saul’s town, though the text does not explain the name further.

verses.text: Ishmaiah the Gibeonite, a mighty man among the thirty and a leader of the thirty; Jeremiah; Jahaziel; Johanan; Jozabad the Gederathite;
verses.arminianNotes: Ishmaiah the Gibeonite, a leader of the thirty, and others are named. Arminian readers note that a Gibeonite holds high rank, perhaps recalling the Gibeonites’ place in Israel since Joshua 9.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Ishmaiah does not appear in the lists of 2 Samuel 23 or 1 Chronicles 11, so his rank among the thirty is known only from this verse. Both traditions read it as honoring a leader whose story is otherwise unrecorded.

verses.text: Eluzai; Jerimoth; Bealiah; Shemariah; Shephatiah the Haruphite;
verses.arminianNotes: Eluzai, Jerimoth, Bealiah, Shemariah, and Shephatiah the Haruphite are named. Arminian readers note the steady listing of names, showing that each man’s commitment was worth recording.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Chronicler preserving the memory of David’s early supporters as part of God’s work. Shared ground: the Haruphite is otherwise uncertain, and both traditions read the verse without speculation.

verses.text: Elkanah, Isshiah, Azarel, Joezer, and Jashobeam, the Korahites;
verses.arminianNotes: Elkanah, Isshiah, Azarel, Joezer, and Jashobeam the Korahites are named. Arminian readers note that the Korahites are best known as Levites, though here they appear among the Benjamite volunteers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the term Korahite may refer to a Levitical family or to another group of the same name. Both traditions acknowledge the uncertainty and read the verse as part of the list of David’s helpers.

verses.text: and Joelah and Zebadiah, the sons of Jeroham of Gedor.
verses.arminianNotes: Joelah and Zebadiah, sons of Jeroham of Gedor, are named. Arminian readers note that the list of Benjamites closes with two more brothers, completing a picture of families joining David.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the conclusion of the first group as testimony to the breadth of support God provided. Shared ground: the location of Gedor is uncertain, and both traditions read the verse as part of the record.

verses.text: Some Gadites joined David in the stronghold in the wilderness, mighty men of valor, men trained for war, who could handle shield and spear; whose faces were like the faces of lions, and they were as swift as the gazelles on the mountains:
verses.arminianNotes: Gadites join David at the stronghold in the wilderness, with faces like lions and swift as gazelles. Arminian readers note the vivid description of their strength and speed as trained warriors.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God supplying David with capable men in a time of need. Both traditions read the imagery as poetic praise of their skill, and note that the stronghold in the wilderness is not identified with certainty.

verses.text: Ezer the chief, Obadiah the second, Eliab the third,
verses.arminianNotes: Ezer the chief, Obadiah the second, and Eliab the third are named. Arminian readers note the careful ranking of the Gadite leaders, showing order and structure among David’s supporters.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the numbered list as honoring each man’s place. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the start of a list of eleven Gadite captains, recorded without further detail.

verses.text: Mishmannah the fourth, Jeremiah the fifth,
verses.arminianNotes: Mishmannah the fourth and Jeremiah the fifth are named. Arminian readers note that the list continues in order, preserving the memory of men otherwise unknown in Scripture.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s attention to individuals in the record of these names. Both traditions read the verse simply as part of the ranked list of Gadite captains, without speculation about the men.

verses.text: Attai the sixth, Eliel the seventh,
verses.arminianNotes: Attai the sixth and Eliel the seventh are named. Arminian readers note that the Chronicler takes care to name every leader, a sign that each one’s decision to join David mattered.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the list as a record of God’s provision through ordinary men of courage. Shared ground: both traditions read the names as historical, honoring service rather than drawing symbolic meaning.

verses.text: Johanan the eighth, Elzabad the ninth,
verses.arminianNotes: Johanan the eighth and Elzabad the ninth are named. Arminian readers note the steady rhythm of the list, which builds a picture of a well-organized band of warriors from Gad.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the orderly ranking as fitting the Chronicler’s interest in structure and leadership. Both traditions read the verse as part of the record of those who came to David before his reign.

verses.text: Jeremiah the tenth, and Machbannai the eleventh.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah the tenth and Machbannai the eleventh complete the list. Arminian readers note that a second Jeremiah appears in the list, showing that names were often shared among Israelites.
verses.reformedNotes: With Machbannai the roll of Gadite officers is finished. Reformed readers simply note the care taken to preserve it, and both traditions decline to find symbolism in the count of eleven.

verses.text: These of the sons of Gad were captains of the army. He who was least was equal to one hundred, and the greatest to one thousand.
verses.arminianNotes: These Gadites were captains, the least equal to a hundred and the greatest to a thousand. Arminian readers note that the phrase may describe their command or their strength, and interpreters read it both ways.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the description as honoring their ability as leaders in David’s forces. Both traditions acknowledge that the expression is open to more than one reading and avoid pressing its exact meaning.

verses.text: These are those who went over the Jordan in the first month, when it had overflowed all its banks; and they put to flight all who lived in the valleys, both toward the east and toward the west.
verses.arminianNotes: They crossed the Jordan in the first month when it overflowed its banks, and routed those in the valleys. Arminian readers note the courage required to cross the river at flood, as in Joshua 3:15.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God enabling the crossing, recalling Israel’s earlier entry into the land. Shared ground: the verse highlights the determination of those who joined David, and both traditions read it as historical narrative.
